By analyzing the structure of thermal entanglement, we demonstrate that the singularities at the thermal Riemann zeta pole encode the thermofield double state's quantum entanglement properties. This finding is further illustrated through analogies with harmonic oscillators and Jordan-Wigner transformations. Additionally, we investigate the Riemann zeta pole's influence on the thermal entanglement spectrum in power-law systems, showing that the pole's location determines the exponent characterizing thermal entanglement. This provides a framework for studying the singularities associated with other thermofield double states. To investigate the long-range behavior of thermal entanglement, we consider a one-dimensional system of this type, demonstrating that its thermal entanglement monotones display power-law behavior, with the specific exponent determined by the system's underlying physics. This is particularly relevant in scenarios where the thermal entanglement properties are indicative of a phase transition or where the entanglement could facilitate the spread of information. This study focuses on a specific category of mechanisms known as the $k$-nearest-neighbor (KNN) mechanism, which has been extensively researched in static systems but remains unexplored in non-trivial network vibrations. To bridge this knowledge gap, we first establish a theoretical framework to analyze the spectrum of KNN networks, yielding a set of linear equations that define the eigenvalues in a specific frequency range. By conducting extensive numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the spectrum of these vibrating networks exhibits distinct behavior, with eigenvalue densities developing into a smooth, continuous distribution as the vibration frequency increases. Additionally, we identify a precise condition – where the eigenvalues lie beneath a curve defined by the square root of the vibration frequency divided by the degree of the network – that determines whether the spectrum is continuous or discrete. Our findings also reveal a significant impact of vibration on the eigenvector centrality of system nodes, with the effect being more pronounced on higher-degree nodes. To further investigate the applicability of our theoretical model, we conduct a supplementary analysis using a protein molecular model, yielding a coherent understanding of the relationship between the vibration spectrum and protein structure. Finally, we explore the practical utility of our research by highlighting potential avenues for further exploration, such as the incorporation of vibration effects into network centrality measures, and the development of more efficient algorithms for generating quasi-random networks. Our study provides a comprehensive insight into the spectrum of vibrating KNN networks, a fundamental precursor to investigating their dynamic properties and behavior over extended periods of time. Since manually labeling objects in images is time-consuming and expensive, many object detection models rely on datasets annotated with bounding boxes by crowdsourcing platforms.  However, the quality of such datasets can vary significantly due to inaccurate annotations.  Current methods assess dataset quality based on the performance of a single model when applied to the dataset, which we believe is an inadequate metric because it evaluates the model's performance rather than the dataset's quality. 

  To develop a more comprehensive understanding of dataset quality, we propose a novel approach that evaluates dataset quality based on the performance of multiple models when applied to the dataset.  Our approach utilizes a diverse set of state-of-the-art object detection models to systematically assess the influence of inaccurate annotations on model performance and the resulting errors. 

  We constructed the Large-Quality Object Detection Dataset (LQOD), which consists of 50,812 images containing partially removed and artificially introduced artifacts at five different severity levels, along with corresponding object annotations.  We employed twelve prominent object detection models to evaluate the impact of quality on model performance and introduced a new metric called the Quality Performance Score (QPS). 

  Our experiments with the LQOD dataset at different quality levels demonstrate that small changes in annotation quality significantly affect model performance, showcasing the limitations of model averaging.  Our results also highlight the inconsistency between model performance and visual plausibility when encountering low-quality images. 

  We released the LQOD dataset and the associated evaluation framework, which include the LQOD-1k (1,000 images with 5% artifacts) and LQOD-50k (50,812 images with 5% artifacts), to support the advancement of robust object detection models. 

  Our approach has the advantage of being easily integrated into existing training pipelines, allowing for the evaluation of dataset quality during training.

The research includes generating intense, coherent electric fields via high-harmonic generation in a nonlinear crystal and successfully pairing an EIT medium with a Josephson microwave circuit. Furthermore, the study shows that even minor changes in the circuit frequency can result in significant alterations to the EIT phenomenon, enabling control of its characteristics.   - A 10% improvement in the depth of EIT phenomenon when the circuit frequency matches the EIT system.

A novel GPU-based implementation of JPDA filtering is presented, which leverages the full potential of modern GPUs to achieve remarkable performance enhancements.  In this research, modern NVIDIA GPUs were utilized as the platform for developing and evaluating the proposed GPU-based JPDA filtering system. In this study, we introduce a novel category of errors known as "rich data exploits," which can derive meaningful statistical insights from partially complete datasets, potentially evading detection by standard data loss functions. We then provide theoretical explanations for these errors and demonstrate their potential to mimic real adverse event patterns. Additionally, we propose a range of synthetic models that can replicate these errors, as well as suggest proactive measures to prevent such errors, including assessing capture system robustness and implementing redundant data collection methods. Our findings stress the importance of treating electronic data capture systems as "double-blind": recognizing that researchers using these systems are unaware of potential flaws while readers should approach trial results with skepticism if capture systems were utilized. Furthermore, we advise researchers to publicly disclose the methods employed by their capture systems, as well as provide access to raw data in order to facilitate verification of trial findings. In instances where such verification is not feasible, we propose that capture systems be treated as a critical component of the research environment, subject to rigorous testing and validation procedures similar to those used for statistical analysis software. We also introduce a novel concept of "robustness of analysis," which refers to the extent to which analysis results are resistant to flaws present in the capture system, and suggest a set of best practices to ensure this robustness, such as conducting regular system audits and implementing data validation checks. By taking these steps, we aim to minimize the risk of rich data exploits and other types of errors that may arise from flaws in capture systems, and to ensure the integrity and reliability of trial data.   Upon reviewing recent advances in robotic learning, we identified a critical barrier that threatens the development of complex robot skills. This issue stems from the insufficiency of highly automated testing tools for robot programs. As a crucial step towards addressing this challenge, we propose categorizing tests into two primary types - logic-based tests and data-driven tests. We further present a system called 'Autotest' that automates the creation, execution and combination of these tests for robot programs written in CLAM. a collaborative editing system can be complex when multiple users are contributing to the same document. A prominent approach involves employing a graph-based system where users are represented as nodes and their collaborative efforts are reflected as edges, based on their decision to accept changes proposed by other users. The challenge lies in identifying valued community members who are sought after for future collaborations. A prominent approach involves using community detection algorithms but is hindered by the lack of understanding of how node degrees are influenced by the acceptance of proposed changes. This paper performs an in-depth analysis of a specific degree profile, associated with the English Wikipedia, in order to uncover the underlying mechanisms of how user collaborations are formed. By using a statistical model called the Exponential Random Graph Model, the unique characteristics of a Wikipedia editor's degree profile are defined as the likelihood of collaborating with particular other editors, based on either shared editing goals or personal relationships. The model reveals that the most desirable collaborators for an editor are typically those with similar interests, often leading to long-term collaborations, whereas personal relationships tend to form more temporary collaborations. The findings provide a deeper understanding of a Wikipedia editor's likely collaborations and can be used to develop more accurate predictive models of collaboration behavior. Furthermore, the unique characteristics of a Wikipedia editor's degree profile, derived from the analysis of how they accept proposed changes, can be employed to enhance existing community detection methods, providing a higher level of accuracy, particularly in cases where a community member's reputation is valued. This capacity for cooperation has enabled humans to achieve remarkable feats and develop complex social structures that are prevalent today. While the value of cooperation is widely acknowledged, it is crucial to understand its underlying motivations and how they evolve over time in different environments of strategic interaction. This study leverages evolutionary dynamics to explore how humans voluntarily cooperate with others in a range of scenarios, as represented by the iterated prisoner's dilemma game. Over multiple iterations, players can choose between cooperative or competitive actions, with the goal of applying policies that result in optimal payoffs through an evolution of learned actions. This research utilizes the neuroevolutionary NEAT algorithm to train agents in both single-player environments, such as a dynamic version of the prisoner's dilemma, and multi-agent environments, such as the aforementioned iterated prisoner's dilemma game. When competing against a fixed opponent, such as a cooperative, neutral, or competitive agent, it was discovered that the evolved policies often reached a state of cooperation. However, when competing against an evolving opponent, neutral or competitive agents were preferred over cooperative agents. Interestingly, it was found that an iterative strategy of exploring and exploiting proved effective in many cases. To further investigate these findings, a theoretical model based on the concept of an adaptive exponential learning rule was developed and showed comparable results to the NEAT algorithm. With this model, as well as a proposed modification for handling continuous action spaces, it is possible to analyze the dynamics of cooperation in great detail. Although this approach was successful in explaining the observed behavior in most of the tested environments, there was an exception - the iterated prisoner's dilemma game with an unbounded score. In this exceptional case, the risk-averse nature of the NEAT algorithm led to a failure in detecting cooperative agents. To address this limitation, it was suggested that the NEAT algorithm could be modified to handle this scenario by introducing a trade-off between the exploration and exploitation of new actions. By leveraging a finite-dimensional representation, we are able to numerically assess the thermodynamic metrics and related quantities. Our findings are demonstrated through a series of examples featuring the harmonic oscillator and hydrogen atom. Additionally, we show that our approach to quantizing thermodynamics aligns with the principles of standard quantum mechanics. Our method employs a two-step process to construct thermodynamic quantities: first, the equilibrium density matrix is computed using a linear combination of basis functions that span the ground state; second, the thermodynamic metrics are calculated by tracing the density matrix and relevant operators. We also introduce an alternative, two-dimensional language to describe thermodynamics, which includes the quantum Euler equation. Within this simplified framework, we verify that our computational method for the quantum Euler equation is accurate. Our study reveals that the quantum Euler equation differs from its classical counterpart due to the impact of spin and the relative significance of canonical and grand canonical ensembles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our computational approach can be employed to model diverse quantum systems. Our investigation highlights that the quantum Euler equation can be accurate provided that the equilibrium density matrix can be expressed through a linear combination of basis functions that span the ground state. Our study also highlights the potential of the harmonic oscillator and hydrogen atom to illustrate fundamental concepts in quantum thermodynamics. Our findings show that for small quasistatic variations in both the harmonic oscillator and hydrogen atom, the difference between the change in entropy and the quantum thermodynamic work is equal to the change in internal energy. Our investigation indicates that this outcome can result from the linear nature of the maps between density matrices that is derived from the linearity of the Schrödinger equation. Our study reveals that the quantum thermodynamic metrics are unaffected by spin when the ground state can be expressed through a linear combination of spin-orbit basis functions that span the ground state. Our study demonstrates that the grand canonical ensemble is more suitable than the canonical ensemble when the change in the average particle number is significant and has an opposite effect on the metric tensor. Our study also indicates that the sign change of the grand canonical ensemble average particle number can lead to a distinct metric tensor, which in turn can result in different thermodynamic properties, as seen with the hydrogen atom. Our study provides a computational approach to assess the quantum thermodynamic work, which can be utilized to examine whether a system in thermodynamic equilibrium can transition to another state of equilibrium through a continuous, irreversible process

mainstay of debate among economists studying search models of unemployment. 
While it's widely accepted that jobless individuals see their situations 
improve through job searches, some researchers argue that searches also 
affect employed workers, influencing the length of their job tenures. 
Until now, most analyses have focused on how job searches affect 
transitions between unemployment and employment, without considering how 
searches affect existing employment relationships. In this study, we develop 
a new method to identify the previously unknown effects of job searches, 
using data from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances. 
Using this approach, we estimate that searches increase the likelihood of 
leaving unemployment for employment, while also likely increasing the 
probability of voluntarily exiting current employment and entering 
unemployment. Interestingly, our findings suggest searches may actually 
reduce the rate at which employment relationships end unexpectedly. 
While our analysis does suggest searches influence how workers change 
jobs, it doesn't support the commonly held belief that searches lead to 
more hires. Instead, our findings imply searches may actually increase 
the likelihood of quitting a job and then finding another one. 
Ultimately, our study highlights the importance of accounting for 
searches' distinct impacts on unemployment and current employment when 
interpreting data and developing economic theories.

Specifically, we develop nine distinct optimization algorithms based on non-singular $p$-Bellermann matrices, which we demonstrate can be applied to a range of problems, including convex and non-convex optimization, as well as deep learning.  Our innovative activation functions are designed to be user-friendly, easily integrable into existing neural network frameworks, and available under permissive open-source licenses.  In our experiments, we show the significant improvements provided by these new optimization algorithms, achieving up to a 30-fold reduction in training time and substantially better test accuracy with significantly fewer parameters.  Additionally, we explore alternative applications for $p$-Bellermann matrices in neural network system design.  Our work provides a groundbreaking combination of theoretical innovation and practical achievements, with our code publicly available for download.  We also host a companion video presenting our methods and results in a more engaging visual format.  Further, we co-host a code repository with our collaborators at the University of Kentucky, where we share and develop our optimization algorithms together.  We also successfully mentor and guide multiple undergraduate and master's students to complete their academic projects related to this research. These datasets will comprise a substantial quantity of high-dimensional data, which can lead to computationally expensive and inefficient data manipulation processes if not properly optimized. As such, it is imperative that we develop highly efficient and flexible frameworks for performing in-memory data manipulation efficiently. By utilizing shared memory access, this will enable multiple processing threads to work together seamlessly to handle even the most demanding datasets. Here, we outline a comprehensive approach for creating multi-threaded data frames in memory, which we then apply to a streaming dataset generated by a machine learning model. Our innovative method demonstrates substantial gains in both processing speed and memory efficiency, which we support with empirical evidence obtained from thorough performance assessments. Additionally, we explore cost-reduction opportunities by optimizing memory usage without compromising data accuracy, which further enhances our approach by providing significant improvements while handling large datasets. This, in turn, allows us to process large datasets more efficiently, which we demonstrate with a real-world example. Ultimately, our proposal exhibits improved performance and a significant reduction in memory usage, which we believe will encourage researchers to use data frames extensively in their own projects. By doing so, they can further leverage the computational gains we have achieved. Although we developed a multi-threaded data frame approach, our research is still applicable to a single-threaded environment. However, the performance gains from using multiple threads may vary depending on the available processing cores and system architecture. As such, we recommend using high-performance computers equipped with multiple processing cores for optimal results. This multi-threaded data frame approach can be used to enhance the performance of various machine learning applications that involve large datasets, such as those involving neural networks. However, the gain from using multiple threads may be limited by the memory bandwidth and the computational requirements of the underlying algorithm. This multi-threaded data frame approach can be used to directly improve the performance of batch processing algorithms like TensorFlow and PyTorch. framework for AI systems that mimics the human body's system is proposed.
Comparing the human body to a sophisticated machine made up of interconnected
components highlights the parallels between biology and technology. Utilizing
this metaphor, we introduce a cutting-edge framework for AI development that is
inspired by the human circulatory system. This framework, named Chronos, is an
adaptive and self-configuring cluster that optimizes resource allocation to ensure
maximum performance and efficiency. The Chronos framework utilizes a unique method
of token-based resource management, derived from the human body's use of hormones,
to achieve dynamic resource adjustment. This approach enables the detection and
handling of system imbalances, as well as the adaptation of the system to accommodate
varying workload demands. The results of our experiments demonstrate that the Chronos
framework delivers superior performance in terms of both speed and efficiency. Furthermore,
our analysis reveals that the Chronos approach excels in solving complex optimization
problems and provides valuable insights into the development of distributed AI systems. 
The proposed framework's ability to mimic human hormone systems also paves the way 
for the integration of new fields such as Endocrine Computing where computational 
tasks are triggered by hormonal messages. This may lead to significant gains in 
energy efficiency as we learn from the human body's ability to switch off systems 
during periods of inactivity thus reducing waste in AI system deployments. 
Finally, we introduce the Concept of Intelligence Gradient, a token-based strategy 
for machine learning that mimics the human brain's hierarchical learning mechanism, 
enabling the fusion of heterogeneous learning technologies and making it available 
for use in diverse ML frameworks through a standardized interface. 
This work also welcomes feedback from the community as we seek to further refine 
and expand the proposed framework. 
Throughout this research, we demonstrate the potential of the Chronos framework 
to serve as a cutting-edge, cluster-based solution for AI system deployments, 
utilizing a token-based approach that mimics the human circulatory system. 
This involves developing a dynamic resource allocation system that mimics the 
human endocrine system for optimal performance and efficiency, coupled with a 
method for detecting and addressing system imbalances, as well as a way to 
adapt the system to varying workload demands. 
We showcase the capabilities of the Chronos framework through a series of 
experiments, uncovering its performance and efficiency gains, and gaining insight 
into its ability to tackle complex optimization problems.

This work provides a foundation for understanding the properties of interlocking complete minimal surfaces consisting of multiple helicoids. Furthermore, we establish that any surface of this nature is composed of multiple $M_{\theta}$ manifolds connected by points of non-zero torsion, and that these surfaces are stationary points of the Sacks-Uchida functional when the associated $\theta$ values satisfy a particular symmetry condition. This paper introduces the Self-Supervised Spoken Sentence Stream (S4) model, 
a novel approach that extracts a spoken sentence's embedded meanings from 
acoustic features without relying on manual transcription.  By incorporating 
a masked-language-like loss function and a temporal self-supervised strategy, 
the S4 model learns to summarize the semantic content of spoken sentences while 
masking their audible characteristics.  When tested on the HASHTAG dataset, our 
method demonstrated superior performance to baseline models using manual 
transcriptions, outperforming them by a 25% margin in semantic extraction 
accuracy.  Furthermore, the S4 model's ability to use spoken sentences as 
input enables the creation of a training framework with significantly reduced 
annotation costs, achieving comparable results while reducing the need for 
transcriptions by up to 90%.

network layers possess limited possible values.  This property is referred to as "element-wise constraint" or "channel-wise constraint" depending on the network layer in question.  For example, the constraint for a convolutional layer would apply to the output, while the constraint for a fully connected layer would apply to the input.  We propose a method to systematically identify all possible values for a given layer, thereby concisely representing them as an integer set.  This integer set, denoted as $\mathcal{C}$, serves as a "compact code" for the given layer.  We further develop two specific integer sets: one for binary data and another for multi-class classification that utilizes one-hot encoding.  Based on these integer sets, we create a novel neural network layer called the "quantized layer" that generates a given layer's output while adhering to $\mathcal{C}$.  This is accomplished through the incorporation of an error-boundered differential evolution algorithm, a non-uniformity-reducing decoder, and/or a modified $K$-nearest neighbor classifier, depending on the nature of the constraint.  We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach via the analysis of two real-world datasets.  Specifically, we examine the CNNs and FCNs used in the MNIST dataset and the CNNs used in the 5000-image subset of the Fashion MNIST dataset.  In each instance, we observed a substantial reduction in precision without a notable decrease in accuracy.  This achievement runs counter to current precision optimization techniques that typically overlook the limited possible values of certain neural network layers. Our results provide an extensive range of alternatives for computing the ACs of the gamma function and related functions, spanning from basic integral expressions to more complex representations involving convergent series and product formulations. These alternative expressions can be further subdivided into two categories: those that remain within the original complex sector and those that fall within a adjacent complex sector, often referred to as the "next" sector. These models typically rely on micro-level interactions to influence users' beliefs but can be enhanced by incorporating a macro-level representation of the network's opinion spectrum. We propose a novel approach, the OpSEn, that leverages a position vector to capture the gradual change in opinions among users and allows for the quantification of opinions at any point in time. By expressing the opinion distribution as a function of the position vector and a scaling factor, OpSEn enables efficient computation of the sentiment of any network subgroup. The model can further analyze the public sentiment and perception in a social network by incorporating external influences and opinion shifts from specific network groups. We validate our approach through simulations of two common application scenarios. The first evaluates how OpSEn handles diverse opinions within a dynamic network, while the second involves a network that adapts to external changes in opinion. The results show OpSEn's ability to accurately model the evolution of public sentiment and perception in both situations. The model can be applied to various domains, such as studying the evolution of public opinion in online forums, social networks, and mainstream media, with potential uses in sentiment analysis, leading influencers identification, and opinion diffusion prediction. We make OpSEn's implementation available as an open-source tool. This method relies on the underlying metric structure of the network to determine its topological properties. For networks without a clear geometric representation, this method can be applied by using a proxy metric, such as betweenness centrality. Here, we introduce a new approach, the tube centrality method, which extends the tube method to negatively weighted networks. By utilizing Dijkstra's algorithm with virtual volumes, we develop a new formula for calculating tube centrality, which can be applied to any network that has a potential geometric representation. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a series of empirical studies examining brain networks derived from magnetic resonance imaging data. Our results show that our method produces comparable results to the original tube method while accounting for the negative weights present in these networks. Additionally, we found that our approach has greater than 90% correlation with the existing method in over 90% of the networks studied. Furthermore, we found that our method is more resistant to the variation of networks due to different constructions, which is crucial for accurately modeling real-world networks with negative weights. Finally, we demonstrate that our method may be employed by utilizing a proxy metric, such as load distribution, which is essential for a meaningful analysis of the results. In conclusion, our study provides a novel method, the tube centrality method, for analyzing geometric networks with negative weights, which can be applied to a wide range of fields. Furthermore, this method is accessible online. In this context, the CP (Canonical Polyadic) decomposition is widely employed for data that can be represented as a sum of three-way tensors derived from linear combinations of three mutually orthogonal vectors.  However, for many real-world applications, it is more realistic to assume that data results from a more complex underlying structure, thus necessitating the incorporation of outliers and approximation errors.  In this research, we introduce the _demi-regularized_ CP (d-rcp) algorithm to decompose tensors affected by outliers and approximation errors.  We also develop an alternative to the algorithm known as the semi-regularized CP (s-rcp) approach, which can be seen as an extension of the Gauss-Newton method for least squares.  By analyzing and comparing these two approaches, we aim to contribute to the ongoing discussion on the convergence and properties of the d-rcp algorithm. The frameworks developed in this study can provide valuable insights for designing and monitoring the convergence of more sophisticated tensor decomposition methods. However, since these manifolds typically lack explicit parametrization, Inference becomes a significant challenge.  One particular approach involves defining a local parametrization for a manifold in high-dimensional space, but this can be time-consuming due to the need for extensive data samples.  Another strategy uses a notable set of manifold points with special properties, such as being difficult to distinguish from nearby neighbors.  These unique points can serve as the parameters for a manifold in a lower-dimensional space, allowing for efficient inference by selectively identifying and weighting the most distinctive points for a given task.  One such set of notable points, called the $k$-echo system, has already been shown to capture various structured patterns in data. These findings highlight how the distribution of source properties, such as mass ratio, orbital period, and radial distance from the black hole, vary depending on the initial position and velocity of the inspiral's companion object. These variations are so substantial that they outweigh any differences caused by either the companion object's specific type or the black hole's spin. As a result, when modeling these systems, it's essential to take into account not just the companion object's average properties but also its potential to deviate from those averages. Additionally, any differences caused by either the companion object or the black hole's spin will likely be overshadowed by evolution-driven deviations when analyzing data from such systems. By converting expressions into a graph representation, Greenform provides insights into the composition of formulas that were previously impossible to obtain through conventional means.  As an example of the tool's capabilities, we present an unconventional proof of the associativity property of the differential operator $\partial$ used in the Homogeneous Piecewise Polynomial (HPOL) class of functions, whose formulas range from linear to degree three. By utilizing a technique from geometric measure theory, we rescale the singular set of a generalized harmonic function and examine its dimension in both even- and odd-dimensional scenarios. Our findings include both upper and lower bounds for the dimension of the rescaled singular set, which we demonstrate can differ significantly depending on the number of dimensions. In particular, in spaces with four or more dimensions, the dimension of the rescaled singular set can exceed initial estimates, resulting in a significant implication for the traditional Picard's uniqueness theorem in such situations. Conversely, in spaces with three or fewer dimensions, the dimension of the rescaled singular set aligns with initial estimates. Through counterexamples, we show that both the upper and lower bounds we established for the dimension of the rescaled singular set in spaces with two dimensions are equivalent, which further highlights the significance of a recently revised version of Picard's uniqueness theorem in this specific context. This paper assesses several popular speech coding methods using objective and subjective metrics at various bit rates.  Eight NPAC III-encoded speech samples with corresponding transcripts were used for evaluation.  Each speech sample was rated for quality using a mean opinion score (MOS) obtained from a crowdsourced survey of 100 participants.  The four evaluated speech coding methods are:  CMU SPITE, a proprietary speech coding algorithm;  CMU RITE, another proprietary algorithm;  OPUS, a widely adopted speech and audio coding algorithm;  and LPC, an algebraic coding algorithm.  The evaluation took place at five bit rates (3.85 kbps, 8.85 kbps, 12.75 kbps, 18.75 kbps, and 40 kbps).  The findings indicate that CMU SPITE generally achieves superior or equal quality to the other three algorithms across all evaluated bit rates as measured by MOS scores.  This result is corroborated by lower objective scores for CMU SPITE in four out of five comparison scenarios.  Notably, CMU SPITE outperformed the other algorithms by at least 0.8 on the MOS scale at 3.85 kbps, demonstrating a significant quality gap with even moderate bit rates.  The four algorithms displayed similar performance at higher bit rates (above 12.75 kbps).  The research implies that CMU SPITE may be a suitable alternative for use cases where speech coding is critically important, albeit further testing with diverse speech datasets is needed to confirm these findings. By applying CN, we achieved state-of-the-art results with a single multi-task model, matching the performance of a series of models trained on each task separately. corruptions access to the trained model without compromising data privacy.

  To tackle this issue, this paper introduces a new dataset, NewsOpinions, which
  collects expressed opinions from news articles using two social groups:
  Democrats and Republicans. This dataset consists of 1,000 Amazon Mechanical
  Turk annotations, encompassing 2,000 opinion statements regarding 40 diverse
  topics, with five participants from each social group. Each opinion statement
  receives ratings from three aspects: expresser's political affiliation,
  targeted group, and the statement's neutrality. The data analyzes interpersonal
  disagreements, showing that participants from the same social group generally
  share similar views but also exhibit some diversity. Conversely, opinions
  directed at opposing social groups exhibit greater variability. Our evaluation
  demonstrates that a straightforward strategy incorporating expresser's political
  affiliation and targeted group can yield satisfactory results. This approach
  achieves notable accuracy on a dedicated dataset for political articles,
  outperforming alternative methods. The study's findings also highlight the
  significance of considering the writer's intentions and the reader's perceptions
  of a statement's neutrality. To facilitate further research, the dataset is
  openly accessible via its repository. 

  Pre-trained models like TADQL and ONLION, which attempt to infer opinions
  based on written content, are tested against our dataset, exhibiting limited
  success. This shortcoming is attributed to several issues: the models' reliance
  on shallow techniques, the lack of consideration for the writer's intentions,
  and the neutral nature of many statements, which hinders explicit
  identification. Combining these models with a neutral statement classifier
  yields improved performance. 

  To handle the ambiguity surrounding neutral statements, a proposed approach
  involves leveraging paraphrasing techniques to break them down into more
  manageable components. This is demonstrated through an experiment showing
  significant performance gains when applying this method to the NewsOpinions
  dataset. 

  In addition to evaluating our dataset, we examine the underlying structure
  of opinions expressed in news articles. This analysis reveals that articles
  often contain groups of statements connected by semantic relationships,
  comprising clusters that share similar meanings. Furthermore, within these
  clusters, opinions are often arranged in an orderly fashion, starting with
  general statements and becoming more specific as you move through the sequence.
  This inherent organization can be utilized to guide the process of identifying
  opinions in discourse segments.

. al's research introduced the concept of intra-quantum error correction using the QECC circuit architecture. This study builds upon their finding by demonstrating the practical application of such QECCs through the preparation of parity-checked cluster states via single-qubit operations. Utilizing this method, we demonstrate the transformation of a five-qubit GHZ state - a highly entangled state with distinct stability properties - into its parity-checked counterpart using only single-qubit errors as resources. This process is shown to be feasible even when faced with high levels of noise during the transformation process. Based on this, we propose a protocol for executing precise operations under the protection of QECCs. Additionally, we present the outcomes of simulating this protocol under the influence of both coherent and incoherent errors. These outcomes are obtained through the execution of the proposed protocol using the LionQuantum platform. Furthermore, we compare our results to those obtained from a theoretical model that assumes perfect coherence, as well as with outcomes derived from a metropolitan fiber channel that exhibits both coherent and incoherent degradation. This comparison serves to illustrate the threat of coherent interference to QECCs and the necessity of developing more robust quantum error correction methods. Besides that, we also analyze the impact of replacing a GHZ state with an W state, as well as the outcomes resulting from an increase in the number of qubits while keeping the state's complexity constant. Additionally, we propose the use of a GHZ state with distinct stability properties for intra-quantum error correction, as well as the implementation of a parity-checked toric code based on the preparation of parity-checked cluster states via single-qubit operations. Finally, we point out the threat posed by coherent interference not just to the preparation of states but also to the execution of any quantum algorithm. a field that attempts to develop automatic methods for evaluating the perceptual quality of images.  These methods are crucial for image processing systems that rely on real-world visual input, such as compression and restoration systems.  Deep learning-based approaches have shown significant promise in IQA, but there are concerns about why they seem to perform better when trained and tested on the same dataset.  Our research addresses this issue by introducing a new, all-in-one dataset called the Aligned Large-Size Dataset for IQA (ALSD-QA).  ALSD-QA comprises 50,000 pairs of distorted and undistorted images, along with corresponding quality scores.  These images are drawn from the ALSD-Compression9 dataset, which involves evaluating the perceived quality of super-resolved images produced by compression algorithms.  We compared our findings with two alternative approaches that use the same dataset but employ supervision signals based on mean squared error (MSE) and perceptual quality scores.  We demonstrated that our proposed approach, which uses a quality score supervision strategy, performs better than the alternative approaches by leveraging the ALSD-QA dataset.  We also introduced an innovative method, called the Quality-Gated Adapter Module (QGAM), for IQA that builds on the quality score supervision strategy.  This approach involves creating a quality-gated adapter module that incorporates quality scores from a fixed-range Gaussian distribution.  We evaluated our approach on the ALSD-QA dataset and found that it performs better than the state-of-the-art IQA baselines.  Our research provides a new comprehensive dataset and a novel adaptive mechanism for IQA that can be applied to a broader range of image processing tasks.  We believe that our findings will serve as a reference point for future research on unsupervised IQA methods.  Our approach also has the potential to be applied in practice, as demonstrated by compression system tests, which show that our approach performs better than baseline approaches.  Our research is significant because it addresses the issue of data efficiency in IQA.  We demonstrated that our approach performs better when trained on a smaller dataset that is half the size of the training dataset for the compression algorithm.  Our research is critical for developing image processing systems that rely on real-world visual input, as shown by compression and restoration system tests, which indicate that our approach performs better than baseline approaches when trained without supervision.  Our research provides a new comprehensive dataset and a novel adaptive mechanism for IQA that can be applied to a range of image processing tasks, including compression and restoration.

mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media. This method accommodates two types of fractures - those that coincide with the mesh edges and those that do not. For the former, we employ standard interface elements, while for the latter, we propose a technique using 'embedded' finite elements within a subdomain. This technique leverages a specialized 'cut' element formulation tailored to areas near fracture locations. We provide a formal description of our proposed method and then establish the relevant coercivity and semi-coercivity conditions for our scheme. These conditions enable us to derive a priori error estimates both for the primal and mixed formulations. We also present numerical results as well as an in-depth analysis of our results through various test cases. This work contributes a new, more versatile approach for modeling Darcy flow within a fractured media using a reasonable number of degrees of freedom. Recognizing the usually vast resolution required to accurately capture fracture surfaces, our method offers a more efficient and simpler to implement solution for such complex systems. This work can serve as a starting point for future extensions, such as handling two-phase flows or nonlinear fracture surface models.

broader theory of linearization for algebraic $K$-theory spectra. This paper initiates the investigation of doubles within the context of stable homotopy theory over a general base ring $R$. For each base ring $R$, the doubles functor establishes a correspondence between $R$-algebras and $R$-linear spectra, serving as a fundamental relationship that encompasses both geometric and homotopy theoretic aspects. This study focuses on both the algebraic and homotopy theoretic properties of doubles, with key results including the derivation of the flat cover of a $R$-algebra through the homotopy type of its doubles, as well as the discovery of connections between the doubles of $R$-algebras and $R$-linear spectra and the corresponding groups within the Morita category of $R$. Additionally, this research identifies instances where the doubles functor preserves or sends preserved properties to or from the corresponding groups, with results ranging from flatness to Morita-Miller-Mack extensions. This investigation also extends previous findings related to the base ring $R = \mathbb{Z}$ by both generalizing and broadening the scope of applicable $R$-algebras. Lastly, this study demonstrates the relevance of these findings to the interpretation of linearization in $K(R)$. This interpretation is based on a linearization functor $\Lambda_R$ that maps an $R$-algebra to the homotopy type of the doubles of $R$ for $R = \mathbb{Z$ or a finite field, or a subfield of $K(R)$ with the property of being closed under multiplication and division, with further characteristics that include continuity, homotopy invariance, and the ability to produce extended $K$-theory spectra through the application of linearization. This study successfully demonstrates the applicability of linearization to effectively overcome the limitations imposed by the Fr\"ohlich's conjecture by providing counterexamples to the latter's surviving aspect, namely the aspect concerning nilpotent $R$-algebras, with the use of the developed homotopy theoretic approach and the employment of the developed language of $R$-linear homotopy theory. Moreover, this study explores the relation between the application of linearization and the problem of determining $K(R)$. This investigation reveals that the general case of determining $K(R)$ remains an open problem with an associated section provided in the appendix, along with additional counterexamples and the discussion of related works

Although such approaches are effective in preventing system failures, their limitations in fully simulating real-system dynamics have been acknowledged. Our research aims to provide a multi-component simulation framework called "SimGrid/Skel", which offers high-performance concurrency and flexibility, particularly useful for testing complex distributed systems. 

  Methods: "SimGrid/Skel" leverages the strengths of existing simulation frameworks like SimGrid to enable the evaluation of concurrent, distributed programs comprising multiple components. By utilizing a hierarchical, component-based structure for program representation, users can easily add or remove components and observe resulting performance effects. Additionally, this structure enables the detection of system failures and their causes, allowing for performance optimization efforts to be directed at specific components. 

  Results: Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate the performance and utility of "SimGrid/Skel", showcasing its applications in validating a concurrent search algorithm and optimizing a distributed stream processing system. 

  Conclusion: As systems continue to evolve with the incorporation of concurrent and distributed elements, there is a growing need for comprehensive performance analysis and optimization tools. Programs with multiple, interconnected components require a higher level of abstraction and a more rigorous testing methodology, necessitating a simulation-based approach that excels in overall system understanding.  "SimGrid/Skel" serves this purpose by providing a multi-component simulation framework that excels in observing the interaction between system components, facilitating a deeper comprehension of system performance. 

  Availability: The "SimGrid/Skel" framework is an extension of the established simulation framework SimGrid, available for download at https://skel.simgrid.org/, along with its source code and demonstration programs. 

  Contact: Users can obtain support, share their experiences, and get assisted with using the "SimGrid/Skel" framework through its community forum at https://forum.simgrid.org/. 

  Supplemental Materials: Additional results, experiment settings, and related data can be found in the "SimGrid/Skel" framework's documentation at https://skel.simgrid.org/docs/.

In such cases, numerical diagonalization typically produces power-law fits for energy levels and wave function properties, but these vary depending on the specific system and its scale-free nature. This study presents a theoretical framework that derives power-law behavior for various physical quantities, including energy level spacing, density fluctuations within localized states, and average wave function amplitude, all in terms of the system's size and frequency. Our results highlight the differences caused by the distinction between quasicrystalline and amorphous structures, revealing the impact of these differences on the scaling of energy levels and wave function properties. We develop this concept further by showing that a similar efficient solution exists for calculating expectations of arbitrary observables in these systems. This finding is built on the foundation of quantum simulation, and employs a crude approximation in which only a limited number of Hamiltonianian matrix product operator (MPO) modes are retained, resulting in a well-conditioned MPO. We demonstrate that this approach allows for efficient computation of physical quantities such as energy or position expectations, and demonstrate the practical application of this approach to a model of fermionic particles defying approximation with exact precision. 

  Interestingly, the efficiency of this algorithm is contingent on having access to a specific type of quantum circuit known as the efficient "isometry" that underlies the quantum simulation, and we investigate properties of this circuit, particularly its "matchline" part that determines the conditional probability with which the simulation becomes entangled.

  Finally, we show that this second algorithm can be modified to approximate any quantum circuit efficiently, provided it does not produce an unmanageable amount of entanglement, and we propose that this could be used to study the scalabilty of quantum circuits with exact precision. 

  However, it remains unclear whether this would be of much practical use, as it would require the ability to efficiently simulate the entanglement properties of any quantum circuit, which is generally considered an unsolvable problem. 

  Nonetheless, this does raise an intriguing possibility, and we plan on exploring this further by investigating how well this simulation captures the conditional probability distribution of the entanglement properties of any quantum circuit, which would provide valuable insights into the types of circuits that are capable of producing an unmanageable amount of entanglement.

By introducing a new definition of a singular solution and conducting an in-depth analysis of the equation's properties at the damage site, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions that exhibit switching behavior. Additionally, we find that for equations with switching properties, the damage at a singular point actually reduces to a reflection symmetry. This finding is then confirmed by numerical simulations using a leg-endpoint damage configuration, where the equations' properties are observed to transition from non-singular to singular as the damage depth is decreased. The influence of fractional order on the emergence of singular solutions is also explored, showing that for some equations, singular solutions can emerge externally due to the fractional filter effect. We demonstrate that choice of coordinate gauge significantly impacts the computational scheme and, for optimal results, recommend a specific coordinate gauge.  By utilizing this gauge, we develop an innovative perturbation theory that efficiently handles the computational challenges arising from the wave's high frequency.  We then apply this approach to compute the leading order corrections to the Weyl scalar $\psi_4$ in two distinct scenarios:  an intermediate mass ratio binary black hole merger with high energy effects and a high mass ratio inspiral with specific frequency parameters.  For these scenarios, we evaluate various gauge-dependent metric components and find them to be highly sensitive to the chosen gauge.  However, we find that our preferred coordinate gauge minimizes this sensitivity, resulting in more manageable gauge fluctuations.  Additionally, we observe that the complex oscillations typically associated with gravitational waves cause significant $h_{\mu\nu}$ gauge variations, leading to an understanding that these fluctuations are an inherent feature of the gravitational wave gauge.  We also develop a simpler, gauge-dependent approximation for $\psi_4$ that aligns with our more rigorous analysis, and find this approximation to be directly applicable to standard black hole mergers.  With this approach, we are able to achieve more accurate on-shell conditions and, as a result, significantly improve the calculation of waveform parameters when the frequency parameter $\chi$ is large.  This advancement leads to an observation that mass and charge ratios can influence wave pattern matches, an effect more pronounced in high mass ratio mergers.  We further find an accurate correspondence between the frequency parameter $\chi$ and their implications for gauge-dependent metrics, and observe that specific frequency parameters $\chi$ can either be greatly amplified or mitigated by the configuration of the binary merger or inspiral.  As this analysis seeks to inform the development of next-generation gauge-fixed gravitational wave waveform models, we recommend a distinction in nomenclature between "gauge-dependent" and "gauge-invariant" quantity waveform elements.  With this understanding, we provide a framework and suggestions for several prominent waveform model development groups to consider, including how to effectively utilize side information from the strong-gravity regime of scalar field perturbations.  As such, we also raise the question of whether existing gauge-invariant quantity relationships still hold as accurately as previously reported, and if not, what implications this has for waveform inference studies. Nevertheless, there's a lack of data about wireless usage patterns from a telecommunications perspective. This study analyzes 12 months' worth of data from university campuses, gathering 1055 measurements of wireless usage from various internet service providers, including small businesses and higher education institutions. The findings reveal that data transmission and reception exhibit a strong power-law distribution, with usage varying significantly across different times of day and months of the year. It was discovered that during peak hours, there's a significant drop in data transmission, with a pronounced skewness in usage. This pattern varies depending on the institution and internet service provider in question. Leading factors in data transmission included online file storage, streaming and downloads, along with email usage and internet browsing. The research uncovers new insights into the nature of wireless usage, which can inform optimization strategies for reducing congestion and minimizing costs. Along with this research, the providers are giving out free open data which can be used by other researchers to study other types of internet usage.

of single top quark production in the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider
(LHC). The analysis considers several top quark production scenarios, including those
where the extra dimension affects the behavior of all particles or only the behavior
of gravitons. The search employs a 8 TeV proton-proton collision dataset with an

the expected background variation. The search does not observe any significant excess
beyond the predicted background and sets 95% confidence interval limits on the
production cross-section of single top quarks, which range from 2.2 to 3.0 pb,
depending on the assumed properties of the extra dimension. These limits represent
the most stringent constraints to date on the production of single top quarks through
the influence of an extra space-time dimension.  The study also sets 95% confidence
interval limits on the effective coupling of the weak bosons to the top quark, which
range from 0.188 to 0.436, depending on the assumed properties of the extra dimension. 
These limits also provide the most stringent constraints to date on the effective
coupling of the weak bosons to the top quark.

This note shows that the same technique can be applied to establish the strong completeness theorem for classical first-order logic directly.  This, in turn, allows us to derive both the compactness theorem and the standard completeness theorem for classical first-order logic.  The use of the strong compactness theorem avoids the need to employ Boolean algebra techniques. This method, however, requires the use of the Lowenheim-Skolem theorem in its downward form.  The notes included provide an elementary overview of relevant first-order logic meta-theorems for both propositional and quantificational logic, covering both the basic theorems and their proofs.  This material is intended for students who have previously learned the material covered in the notes.  The purpose is to provide further insight into the underlying reasoning behind these theorems as well as the techniques used to prove them.  This should ultimately enable students to establish these theorems on their own.  The notes cover both the compactness and strong completeness theorems for classical first-order logic.  They also compare these theorems to corresponding theorems for intuitionistic first-order logic.  The notes begin with an overview of the relevant meta-theorems for classical propositional logic. This includes an examination of how these theorems are related to each other as well as how they are connected to corresponding theorems for classical and intuitionistic propositional logic.  The notes conclude with a discussion of how the compactness theorem for classical first-order logic can be derived using the strong compactness theorem.  This, however, requires the use of prime extensions of first-order structures that are based on the Mal'cev operation.  The notes also provide counterexamples to show that the strong compactness theorem does not hold for either classical or intuitionistic first-order logic when the set of sentences in question includes identities that are not first-order expressible. These compilations serve as a comprehensive collection of real-world graph datasets equipped with comprehensive attribute sets, thereby facilitating the evaluation of graph attribute learning algorithms. Specifically, they can be utilized in settings where only graph structure data is initially available, and further node attributes are desired, which is a crucial scenario in numerous domains. Experimental studies conducted on 9 diverse real-world graph datasets, obtained from energy systems, structured documents, biological networks, and social networks, demonstrate the effectiveness of various graph attribute learning algorithms, such as graph neural networks, graph attention networks, and vectorized graph attention networks. The energy systems dataset comprises 528 devices with 10 attributes across two areas, obtained from a practical scenario with values between 0 and 100. The structure of the biological networks graph is also similar to a tree graph. The structured documents dataset comprises 500 documents with 7 attributes across two sections, obtained from the Automatic Section Segmentation (AutSS) dataset compilation series, and the social networks dataset comprises 500 users with 7 attributes across two groups

Previous work by Baccelli and Boulo has already established this convergence in the $L^2$ sense for any-dimensional lattices of dimension $d\geq 2$.  Building on their findings, we examine what conditions are required for the expectation of squared discrete second derivatives to converge and find these conditions are more stringent than those for $L^2$ convergence.  For one-dimensional lattices, we show that the expectation of squared discrete second derivatives converges under the condition $d\geq 5$, while for multi-dimensional lattices with $d\geq 2$, we demonstrate that the relevant condition is $d\geq 4$.  Additionally, we derive explicit formulas for the limiting expectations in both one- and multi-dimensional settings.  This research is complemented by counterexamples that highlight the significance of the specified dimensions.  We also explore and dismiss alternative condition specifications, demonstrating that they do not suffice to ensure the convergence of expectations. This outcome is quantified through conditionals on the central limit theorem, and we also establish a lower bound for the convergence rate.  Additionally, we prove that stationary random walk and Levinson-Wald type extensions also converge under these conditions. developed globally to contain the spread of COVID-19 through strategic localization of users. These apps rely on users providing their geographical location for effective containment strategies. As a trade-off for providing location information, users expect transparent operating principles from the tracing apps. Research indicates that several tracing apps worldwide have encountered controversy due to their opaque operating methods. In this research, we analyze the privacy policies of twenty-one contact tracing apps developed in response to the COVID-19 outbreak in Australia. Our policy review was conducted in accordance with the Australian Privacy Principles (APPs). We discovered that although the majority of the apps in question collect location data from the users, many fail to clearly communicate this information in their privacy policies. As a consequence, there is a discrepancy between what the apps actually collect from the users and what is stated in the privacy policies. We identified two primary categories of data being collected by these apps without explicit user consent: personal information, technical information, and sensitive data. We also developed a rating system to evaluate the data collection practices of the apps and assigned a privacy score to each of the twenty-one contact tracing apps. Our analysis reveals that many of these apps fail to adhere to the Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) and as such, we are presenting our findings to the community with the aim of stimulating further discussion on the subject matter. Additionally, we are making our data collection visualization publicly available to raise awareness about the data collection practices of these apps and promote better data collection methods that are transparent, secure, and adhere to the applicable privacy principles. As the primary contribution of this research, we are presenting a comprehensive overview of the data collection practices of the twenty-one contact tracing apps developed in Australia, and as the secondary contribution, we are making available the associated data collection visualization. As the tertiary contribution, we are prescribing a set of requirements that the Australian government could utilize to develop more effective data collection practices among Australian citizens. Furthermore, we are suggesting that the Australian government implement an integrated data collection management system to effectively monitor the data collection practices of these apps and as such, we are proposing a framework that the government could employ to accomplish this goal. As the final contribution, we are suggesting possible research directions that could stem from this study. As the additional contribution, we are highlighting the privacy scores of the contact tracing apps and as such, we are presenting the data collection practices of the twenty-one contact tracing apps developed in Australia with the aim of stimulating further discussion on the subject matter. As the aim of this research, we are stimulating discussion among researchers and the broader community

This study addresses the issue of effortless programming by introducing a novel approach called Comprehensible Structured Learning for High-Quality Programmers (C-Shaq).  C-Shaq takes a simplified, English-like program description from the user and generates a precise, industry-standard program based on this input.  This process is facilitated by a let-it-break policy, which allows the user to focus on a single instruction at a time, resulting in a hierarchical program composition through a log-like execution trail.  A key feature of C-Shaq is its use of structured learning, where a single instructor program is extracted from multiple user-provided examples, enabling the learning of abstract syntactic components and their combinations from first-order logic descriptions.  Our findings reveal that C-Shaq can both extract and execute complex algorithms, such as sorting and searching, as well as generate basic syntactic programs, such as filtering and mapping. In this study, we introduced a novel algorithm called Deep Tissue Multi-scale Matching (DTMM) for Automatic Cortical Detoxification Mapping. This algorithm was used to create a dataset for comparing automatic and user-guidance derived mapping results. To set up the experiment, a standard multi-session cortical registration method was employed to register a normal brain with 5 abnormal counterparts derived from the same brain after it had undergone detoxification. A widely accepted benchmark, the precision of landmark identification, was selected to evaluate our results. To determine the variability of the baseline, the precision of landmark identification was calculated for each of the 5 sessions at 10 different stages of the registration process. The results showed that our automatic DTMM algorithm produced the same level of accuracy as the user-guided approach. Recently, Guo, Shain, and the second author successfully demonstrated that, within certain classes of groups, profinite equations enable the accurate determination of subgroup multiplicativity, a fundamental property of groups. In this research, we specifically examine the class of abelian groups and prove that multiplicativity of subgroups can be characterized by a single profinite equation. This finding leads us to conjecture that, in fact, all subgroups of abelian groups satisfying the multiplicativity property are reachable via some profinite construction. We support this hypothesis by proving it to be an equational property of abelian groups satisfying the BMF. Additionally, we explore and generalize our results to various other fundamental properties of groups. These developments have significant implications, given that Guo and Shain previously demonstrated that, in contrast to some other properties, neither order nor index is an equational property of abelian groups. Our work employs an innovative combination of techniques, including the utilization of the RZG-Zimmermann ZG-expressions to handle some fundamental properties of groups. Furthermore, we establish that, in all cases where our results hold, they also hold for the more general context of ordered groups. Finally, we provide counterexamples illustrating that, in some instances, multiple profinite equations are needed to characterize a given property, as well as examining the zeno property which emerges from our analysis. These findings collectively enrich our understanding of the profinite construction of groups and their properties.

Our current research expands on this by investigating  what happens when these independent measures are replaced with completely  dependent measures, all belonging to the same particular class, which we'll call  $Q$-dependent measures. We've established that regardless of whether these measures  are defined over a finite or infinite space, they will always result in a measure  that maintains the same statistical efficiency properties as the original measures. the presence of unearned wealth. To answer this, we examine how different social
groups are affected by economic expansion in a world where some individuals hold
substantial wealth, leading to reduced spending on behalf of the wealthy due to
disutility from excessive consumption. In this framework, we find that the wealthy
experience some gain, but the extensive nature of poverty is exacerbated as the
middle class sees only marginal benefit from economic growth.  Analyzing the stock
market, we observe that the value of wealth actually increases at a greater rate than
economic expansion, largely due to the concentration of wealth.  Additionally, we
reexamine the concept of a "trickle-down" effect, finding it to be inaccurately
named as the benefits of economic growth primarily accrue to the wealthy, with the
term more accurately describing the distribution of wealth through reduced spending
among lower-income individuals.  Finally, we propose that a more fitting moniker
for this phenomenon would be a "trickle-up" effect, acknowledging that wealth
indeed plays a central role in this process.  Through dynamic general equilibrium
modeling, we quantify the "trickle-up" effect as the wealthy deriving approximately
seven times the benefit from economic growth compared to the middle class, with
some forms of unearned wealth generating as much as thirty-nine times more benefit
for the wealthy at the expense of the middle class.  Furthermore, we find that
different types of unearned wealth can exhibit varying degrees of concentration,
correlation with consumption, and impact on economic dynamics, resulting in distinct
"trickle-up" effects.  Overall, our research reveals this "trickle-up" effect to be a
widely occurring phenomenon that can promote wealth inequality.  We also propose
measuring the "trickle-up" effect as a utility ratio to facilitate comparison and
analysis of different types of unearned wealth, with the understanding that some
forms may be more effectively concentrated, as exemplified by wealth, in contrast
to others, as seen with income due to labor.  Moreover, our study highlights the
importance of distinguishing between income and wealth, with the latter often
resulting in reduced consumption among the wealthy and therefore greater benefits
for further wealth accumulation, giving rise to a more pronounced "trickle-up"
effect.  We provide several practical policy implications resulting from our analysis
of the "trickle-up" effect, with related models and data available upon request.

, we examine the impact of varying
the anisotropy of Euclidean spacetime on the calculation of baryon number nonconservation
in the presence of non-zero chemical potential. Our findings indicate that
accurate results for this quantity can be obtained when the anisotropy has a minimal
impact, roughly amounting to around 1% relative to total lattice spacing.
This optimal anisotropy may be crucial in future lattice simulations aimed
at precisely measuring baryon number nonconservation. Other aspects of the
simulation, such as the purity of configurations and source lengths, have a more
substantial effect on the already established values of this quantity.  Since
nonconservation of baryon number is primarily driven by the motion of quarks and
gluons, we also investigate its variation with different levels of spatial anisotropy.
This investigation reveals that quark and gluon currents behave asymmetrically in
response to anisotropy, leading to distinct average orientations and a resulting
difference in the calculated rate of baryon number nonconservation. These effects
can be understood through a simple vector model that accurately replicates our
simulation data. This model can be employed to anticipate the effect of future
lattice simulations' parameters on the already established values of this quantity. 
For instance, we anticipate that a 10% enhancement in spatial lattice spacing at
zero chemical potential would lead to an approximately 5% increase in the calculated
rate of baryon number nonconservation. Moreover, our analysis suggests that the
already established values of this quantity may be susceptible to variations of
this magnitude, which could have implications for the interpretation of future
experiments. These findings are relevant not just for lattice simulations but also
have broader implications for the study of strong interaction dynamics.

systems based on prime coding modulation (PCM) have shown significant potential for accurate depth sensing, especially in systems with limited access to light sources (e.g., indoor environments with minimal artificial lighting). ToF systems using PCM benefit from resistance to interference and the ability to measure signal propagation time with high precision. However, there is a trade-off between measuring time-of-flight and decoding the signal, with a balance required between these metrics to achieve optimal performance. Current research primarily utilizes high-power transmitters and advanced modulation schemes to compensate for the limitations of low light, focusing on scenarios with minimal artificial lighting. To address this issue, we introduce a novel ToF PCM approach utilizing optical feedback to enhance signal detection in low-light environments. This approach takes advantage of the optical feedback to infer the transmitted prime sequence, minimizing the impact on neighboring systems. Furthermore, we developed an open-source tool to analyze the performance of our ToF PCM system and applied it to evaluate the proposed optical feedback scheme. Resource expenditure for each system was quantified in terms of the required transmission power, interference generated, and data decoded. To test the proposed scheme, we designed and fabricated an ToF PCM board utilizing an optical feedback system based on a 40 Gbaud PCM system. Experimental results showed that the proposed scheme could maintain high accuracy in depth sensing with 15 times better energy efficiency compared to a non-optical feedback scheme. To address interference concerns, we found that the proposed scheme could decode data in an ToF PCM system with 10 dB lower signal-to-noise ratio. A comparative analysis of the two schemes was provided in terms of power expenditure, interference generated, and data decoded. To facilitate further research, we introduced an open-source ToF PCM system model, publicly available on GitHub. This model was utilized to evaluate the proposed optical feedback scheme and could be applied to other ToF PCM systems based on PCM. Although traditional numerical methods are widely employed for coordination analysis, they become computationally expensive when applied to larger power networks. Moreover, they require initial guess values for convergence, which can be challenging to obtain. On the other hand, fault currents in an uncoordinated system are often underestimated, which may lead to overly optimistic results. This paper proposes an innovative approach to coordinate protective devices using evolutionary algorithms, eliminating the need for complex numerical methods. By applying this method to the IEEE 68-bus test system, we have obtained more accurate results in a significantly shorter computation time compared to traditional methods. The outcome shows that our algorithm not only enhances convergence speed, but also provides a more precise solution by considering all equipment simultaneously, thus reducing the risk of local minima traps. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that traditional methods may fail to provide coordinated settings for certain devices, leading to an inability to analyze system stability during electrical faults without costly numerical methods. On the other hand, our algorithm offers the flexibility to incorporate various objective functions tailored to different system conditions, such as peak stress avoidance and rapid system recovery. Ultimately, our method can serve as a crucial solution for large-scale power networks where traditional methods fall short due to computational limitations.

class of hybrid systems that incorporate events and clock variables to capture behaviors in both discrete and continuous time domains. They have been extensively studied for their formal verification properties, but a significant gap in the research exists for their quotient structures. This study aims to investigate events and clock variables as first-class citizens in the context of hybrid systems, using event-clock automata as a representative example. We demonstrate that combining events and clock variables yields complex behaviors with rich expressive power, but also prone to unexpected complexities in their temporal properties. For instance, the regularity of finite event-clock automata over ordered words relies on the presence of both events and clock variables. Our research also highlights that incorporating clock variables can complicate the reachability analysis of hybrid systems. To facilitate future research, we provide a systematic overview of event-clock automata, covering their definition, regularity properties, and the behavior of their networks. This overview can serve as a foundation for investigating more sophisticated hybrid systems that incorporate events and clock variables. Furthermore, we offer a set of tools and protocols for defining and working with event-clock automata, along with their underlying theoretical foundations. These protocols include algorithms and proofs for the regularity properties of finite event-clock automata, as well as protocols for analyzing hybrid systems defined by event-clock automata. We have implemented these protocols in an accompanying tool and make it available for download. Our study also raises new research directions and complications in the analysis of complex hybrid systems that incorporate events and clock variables. It highlights the necessity to reevaluate existing understanding and algorithms for these systems, as well as the need to develop new theories to address event and clock variables consistently. Our definition and reference implementation of protocols and tools for event-clock automata are now open-source and freely downloadable from the specified website. Our study also includes a set of example use cases and test cases that demonstrate the capabilities of these tools and protocols. These use cases cover a range of scenarios, from simple regular language recognition to more complex reachability analysis in hybrid systems. They employ a range of techniques, such as the ones described in sections 4 and 5, to define and analyze event-clock automata. Our study and these tools and protocols provide a foundation for further research on the theoretical properties of hybrid systems that incorporate events and clock variables. They also provide a toolset for testing and evaluating the temporal properties of these systems. We complement our theoretical findings with numerical experiments, showcasing the superior performance of StiLM in comparison to StiC and standard optimization algorithms.
