This study employs a statistical approach to examine the claims made by Reus and Schulz (2007) and Kumar and Kumar (2019) regarding the benefits of context-based learning for improved student performance. Our data, obtained from three independent sources, consists of grades from over 870 students who were taught the same programming material with either a standalone or integrated approach. Our analysis involved collecting and anonymizing performance metrics from 102 students, with the assistance of a statistical software program, in order to conduct an between-groups design analysis. Our results showed no significant difference in performance between the two learning methods, according to a majority of the metrics we employed. Notably, we discovered a significant positive relationship between the amount of time spent on an assignment and the desired outcome when using the integrated approach, but this relationship was not as clearly beneficial with the standalone approach. Our study offers new insights that could guide educators who wish to explore the claimed advantages of context-based learning visually. Our analysis also highlights potential limitations and areas for further research, such as the possibility of biased outcomes due to sampling methods and the lack of control groups, as well as the relatively small sample size used in this study. Additionally, we provide a replica of the analysis that could be replicated by other researchers, in line with the principles of open science. Overall, our study offers a critical assessment of the claims made by Reus and Schulz (2007) and Kumar and Kumar (2019) and provides metrics that could be employed in future studies, with results that suggest a possible positive relationship between student performance and the use of a more comprehensive learning approach. Previously proven convergence conditions are verified through theoretical and experimental methods. Three specific examples are provided to illustrate the application of these conditions. A preliminary experimental analysis, conducted using a sub-sample of solved equations, reveals that the specified conditions are sufficient to guarantee L^1 convergence. To further analyze the behavior of the methods under study, the condition of monotone stability is established for a range of nonlinear equations and the convergence of the methods in the L^1 norm is confirmed through the application of a well-ordering point theorem. Experimental data, obtained by increasing the accuracy of the random walk method, confirms that the methods converge at the rate of O(h^2). In addition, a comparison of results highlights that the random walk method delivers more precise solutions than the Crank-Nicholson method for certain types of equations. Ultimately, this research provides a set of sufficient conditions to guarantee the L^1 convergence of the random walk method in combination with conservative differences schemes. By building on existing knowledge of the strong stability and convergence properties of the methods under study, this research aims to explore the practical implications of these properties. Keywords: random walk method, conservative differences schemes, L^1 convergence, nonlinear differential equations. 

Abstract:

In this work we investigate the L^1 convergence of numerical solutions obtained from the random walk numerical method, in conjunction with conservative differences schemes, for one-dimensional second-order nonlinear differential equations with monotonicity conditions. Previously proven convergence conditions are verified through theoretical and experimental methods. Three specific examples are provided to illustrate the application of these conditions. model and Random Phase Approximation to calculate vibrational frequencies for
semiconductors with complex structures, such as compound materials and
molecules. The TB model provides a reasonable representation of electronic
behavior with a relatively limited number of atoms, while the RPA accurately
accounts for electron correlations and potential lattice effects. By combining
these methods, our calculations can predict vibrational frequencies with a
high degree of accuracy, even in structures composed of multiple atomic
species. To facilitate future applications, our TB model and phonon
calculations are implemented in the QuantumATK software, accompanied by a
brief guide on how to set up and execute these simulations. Examples are
provided to demonstrate the accuracy of our methods through comparisons
against experimental data and other theoretical predictions. Additionally, our
calculations explore the structural properties of several semiconducting
materials, including BN nanotubes, graphene with adsorbed molecules, and
silicon-based interfaces, highlighting the potential of this approach to
analyze complex materials and interfaces. The associated code is freely
accessible and can be modified to adapt our methodology for use with other
method frameworks.  The source code used for this project is available via a

By developing a customized actor-critic algorithm based on the widely-used Adam optimization method and categorical action selection for binary classification problems, our research indicates that ANNs can effectively learn to control their own optimization process.  We demonstrated this by modifying the algorithm to work with binary data sets, such as the MIS dataset, where ANNs can learn to optimize their own weights through RL, surpassing traditional optimized algorithms.  Specifically, our results show a significant improvement in accuracy on the MIS dataset using the revised algorithm, achieving a mean square error of 0.061, compared to 0.103 for the baseline, as well as a 10% increase in accuracy on certain data sets.  We also observed that our method takes substantially longer to train, specifically requiring 160 epochs to achieve an accuracy of 77.2% on the MIS dataset, compared to 42 epochs for the baseline.  Nevertheless, our findings highlight the potential for further research into neural network optimization methods.  Additionally, we contributed a Python dataset, known as the CNN dataset, for use in studying this topic.  This dataset involves training a linear classifier on the MIS dataset using the revised algorithm.  We anticipate that our method will be applicable to other optimization algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent, and encourage researchers to explore similar work in multi-class scenarios.  We have made our code and dataset available for public access.  With this achievement, we aim to facilitate discussion on the self-optimal training of neural networks.  Although ANNs can effectively learn to control their own optimization process, as evidenced by our results, this approach is largely inefficient when compared to traditional algorithms.  Therefore, we question whether this capability is worth the cost, capturing the essence of the efficiency vs. capability paradox.  This conundrum is an ongoing topic of exploration in the field of artificial intelligence, wherein sudden changes in system behavior are known to occur with minimal changes in system parameters.  We believe that the self-optimal training of neural networks presents a unique and intriguing example of this phenomenon, warranting closer examination through theoretical analysis as well as experimental studies. whose occurrence or magnitude may be influenced by an endogenous event, like a job loss, which in turn is affected by the treatment.  Causal effects of this kind require techniques that account for the complex relationships between treatments, underlying causes, and subsequent effects.  We demonstrate that under specific conditions and using a particular type of model, where the duration of casual mechanisms can vary and there is no hidden component, we can estimate the average causal effect on the duration of a specific outcome by measuring the effect on a corresponding quantity (e.g., the effect of a job loss on unemployment duration is the same as the effect of a change in unemployment status on post-change unemployment duration).  However, this approach is limited to providing a current status estimate and cannot be used to obtain a causal effect on a future state (e.g., estimating the effect of a layoff on future unemployment is impossible).  We also show that if we assume that the causal mechanisms operate independently over time and that there are no hidden components, we can estimate the average causal effect on a variable with time-varying components by using a corresponding quantity, but this is only possible if the duration of the causal mechanisms is independent of past events.  We present two applications: estimating the effect of a job loss on subsequent depression and analyzing the effect of unemployment on subsequent cardiovascular events.  The results show that a job loss increases subsequent depression in 27.5% of cases and has no significant effect in the second example.  We also offer guidance on instrumental variable techniques for tackling similar research questions.  We demonstrate that under specific conditions, using an instrument that affects treatment choice but not the outcome and does not influence the underlying causes of the outcome can be used to estimate the average causal effect on a variable with time-varying components, but this approach may not work if the instrument influences the duration of the causal mechanisms or hidden components, which in turn affect the outcome.  We show that unemployment, as defined by the CPS, is not independent of past events and does not reflect current economic conditions, which is confirmed by other researchers using alternative definitions of unemployment.  We also present the outcomes of attempting to use instrumental variable techniques to estimate the effect of a job loss on subsequent depression.  The results show that some instruments have a significant effect on the propensity to experience depression within a year but do not improve the estimation when using IV techniques due to issues like strong feedback or the instrument having a significant effect on future unemployment which in turn affects depression. Although extensive research utilizes the incremental learning approach to develop models, little work examines the underlying structural characteristics of PLMs.  Our study investigates the topological structure of the task and data that underlies the PLMs, which can be viewed as a parameterized manifold.  By leveraging the latent features extracted by the pre-training process, we propose that the manifold incorporates embedded representations of all subsequent NLP tasks, which can be manipulated through the shared parameters that arise from the non-incremental training process.  Our analysis reveals that the parameterized manifold possesses an orderless symmetry, which can be utilized to design innovative methods for both few-shot classification and zero-shot inference.  Specifically, our proposed method for few-shot classification involves maximizing the distance between class samples and integrating the ordered features through the use of a GML loss function, which can be optimized via the sphere loss and hinge loss for relational reasoning.  Our approach to zero-shot inference proposes the use of a general score aggregator, which can be realized through the type-aware multi-layered sum over the latent tree structure parameterized by the BERT model. This approach involves transforming the problem into a stochastic variational equation, achieved by introducing a random field and optimizing the cost function. A Quasi-Monte Carlo method is then employed to approximate the expected value, yielding a manageable computational burden. Key to this approach is the derivation of a tail bound for the Monte Carlo estimation of the expected value, obtained through the application of Kolmogorov's consistency criterion. This bound ensures that the optimal control policy can be determined with a level of precision corresponding to the desired accuracy of the Monte Carlo estimation. A key feature of this method is the development of an iterative procedure for approximating the optimal control policy, obtained by refining the bound on the Monte Carlo estimation error. This approach is demonstrated through the application to two different models of stock price dynamics, for which it yields a closed-form expression for the optimal control policy. This expression is shown to converge at a rate of $O\left(N^{-1/2}\right)$, where $N$ represents the number of Monte Carlo samples, under the condition that the filter of the Geometric Brownian motion is a constant. Otherwise, the rate of convergence is estimated to be $O\left(\sqrt{log(N)/N}\right)$. The computational efficiency of this method is evaluated through a series of Monte Carlo simulations, conducted for both the deterministic and stochastic systems. The results obtained with this method have a rate of convergence of $O\left(N^{-1/2}\right)$ for the Monte Carlo estimation of the expected value, yielding a closed-form expression for the optimal control policy. erial Vehicles (UAVs) is expected to expand significantly in the coming years, driven by growing demand from delivery services, surveillance operations, and photography. As a result, there will be an increasing need for UAV operators to navigate regulatory frameworks regarding flying restrictions. This necessity motivates the development of a system that creates optimized flight paths for UAVs within restricted areas to drop packages at designated delivery points. This package delivery problem can be resolved using a type of graph problem known as the shortest periodic path problem, which can be solved efficiently by expressing the problem in integer linear form. We have tested various instances of this problem representative of real-world package delivery scenarios and found that they can be solved rapidly by computational methods. Additionally, we have found that in many circumstances, the optimal solution involves a simple back-and-forth flight path, which could be implemented more easily in automated systems. These findings have the potential to be built into more complex systems for automated package delivery. 

  We have also begun to explore how periodic paths can be used in multi-UAV delivery situations and have developed a method for creating high-quality periodic paths for individual UAVs, which can be combined to achieve optimal combined paths. This approach has the benefit of being very fast to compute, but may on occasion miss the optimal solution. This work could be further developed to accommodate multiple constraints such as no-fly zones and wind resistance which have significant implications on the delivery time and pose a significant computational challenge to solve optimally. 

  We propose an open-source challenge to encourage the development of more efficient algorithms for these types of problems and have made available a set of test cases for this purpose, which can be used to assess the performance of any new computational method against established benchmarks. These test cases are unique in their size and complexity, offering a significant challenge for any emerging fast-and accurate computational methods to clear the barrier of only being able to solve small instances in a reasonable amount of time.  We hope this challenge and contribution will lead to a leap in the development of more complex automated delivery systems. 

  We have taken the initial steps in solving this problem by identifying different types of periodic paths that could be used for delivery purposes and a new method was presented to create high-quality periodic paths by utilizing existing optimal path solutions. This innovative approach excels due to its ability to handle a large number of vertices without difficulty, however it may on occasion miss the optimal solution.  We hope this discovery will lead to a leap in the development of more complex automated delivery systems.

  In dynamic systems, this requirement leads to an often unfulfilled need for
  developers to provide details about how inputs affect the system's behavior and
  state.  To address this issue, we've created an automated tool to perform a
  linear sensitivity analysis on discrete-time dynamic systems described by their
  state transition matrices.  This tool allows system developers to conduct a
  review of the system's design, assessing the impact of changes in input
  characteristics on system performance and stability.  A case study of a closed-loop
  traffic light system demonstrates the utility of this method.  By applying a
  linear sensitivity analysis, we can quantify the effect of station capacity changes
  – previously considered minor – on the efficacy of this type of traffic light
  control.  Our analysis reveals that, under specific conditions, a increase in
  capacity can actually decrease the mean sojourn time in an intersection. 
  Furthermore, this finding prompts a re-examination of systems designed with
  static models, suggesting that a more in-depth analysis is needed to ensure
  optimality.  We also use this tool to investigate the impact of a significant
  road reconfiguration project in Boston, Massachusetts, where traffic patterns
  have been found to become nonlinear due to changes in road connectivity. 
  Unfortunately, this implies that there's no longer a clear understanding of 
  how changes in input characteristics influence the system's behavior and state. 
  Consequently, this project presents both computational challenges as well as 
  questions about the effectiveness of control strategies designed with static 
  models.  A way to address these challenges is to perform a sensitivity 
  analysis–but doing so is hindered by the lack of a systematic approach for 
  dynamic systems.  We mitigate this limitation by introducing an automated 
  method for calculating the state transition matrix and then leveraging this 
  computation to perform a linear sensitivity analysis. 
  We leverage this analysis to provide policy recommendations to transportation 
  engineers.  Specifically, our results suggest that a traffic light control 
  strategy designed with a static model may not necessarily be optimal when 
  there's a significant change in road connectivity due to different mixing 
  patterns–but we don't yet know the implications of this discovery. 
  We also use this analysis to identify potential data gaps that could delay 
  infrastructure projects by providing a preliminary assessment of a project's 
  potential impact before collecting state data.

A new multi-level contrastive learning method is proposed, where the network is initially pre-trained to extract basic image features, with subsequent training allowing the model to learn branch-specific features while reducing the contrastive loss for the segmentation task. crucial for both routine medical care and complex surgical environments. Traditional pulse oximetry, the standard method for this, relies on a two-wavelength approach to deduce oxygen saturation. Despite widespread adoption, this method has limitations, particularly in cases where baseline signal is low, leading to an increased risk of inaccurate readings. To mitigate these restrictions, alternative approaches have been proposed; one such method involves using multiple oximetry pairs to increase the accuracy of measurements. However, this method also has its drawbacks due to the expense and bulk of the device. To address these issues, we propose a novel approach utilizing a convolutional neural network to predict oxygen saturation directly from raw signal data. Through the use of a large dataset containing a diverse range of signals, our model was able to achieve high accuracy in comparison to traditional methods; one such method involves using the Bergman estimator. Furthermore, our approach was shown to be robust in scenarios with low signal quality, reducing the influence of expensive hardware on the device's overall size. A significant advancement of this work could be the real-time implementation of the proposed model, achieving higher accuracy in scenarios with high motion levels. With this in mind, a preliminary study was conducted to assess the efficacy of the proposed method during life, utilizing data collected from the Physionet MIMIC III database. Following data preprocessing, a significant improvement in performance was observed when using a convolutional neural network in comparison to the Bergman estimator. Although the model performed well on the training and validation sets with low motion levels, a notable drop in performance was experienced with high motion levels. To mitigate this, the use of a technique that combines multiple models was explored; one such approach, the soft voting technique, was found to provide superior results. With this in mind, a notable achievement of this work could be the release of the publicly available PhysioNet Challenge. Based on the evaluation of 500 randomly selected samples from the test set with low motion levels, our model achieved a high correlation coefficient of 0.89. With this in mind, a significant advancement of this work could be the exploration of explaining the predictions made by the neural network. Through the analysis of the data, it was observed that pulse oximetry data exhibits a unique characteristic where predictions made by the model correspond to the median value of the signal rather than the mean. To illustrate this, a visualization of the data was created using a heat map. Despite the promising outcomes, a limitation of this work was the absence of a formal theoretical explanation for how the neural network makes predictions.

The growing interest in using IHP (Integrated Hybrid Precision) training for efficiently training neural networks with mixed precision is, therefore, unsurprising. The concept of IHP involves dividing a network into distinct precision sections where each portion uses either low or high-precision floating point calculations. Research has shown that IHP can achieve comparable accuracy to pure high-precision training while benefiting from significant gains in computational efficiency and memory access benefits. The current body of research focuses primarily on general observations rather than in-depth analyses of how precision affects neural network performance. To gain a more profound understanding, we conducted an in-depth study of how different precision configurations influence various neural network performance indicators during IHP training. Our findings, which can be applied to multiple high-level architectures and dataset combinations, provide a set of guidelines for selecting optimal precision configurations based on desired performance characteristics. These findings also hint at possible explanations for observed behavior and serve as a foundation for future research into the performance characteristics of IHP networks. The implemented framework, which we refer to as Precision Explorer, is an open-source tool that allows for the comprehensive evaluation of IHP models and is available for download at this GitHub repository. This method involves applying the method of stationary phase to a formally integral representation of the solution. A key component in achieving this involves transforming the integral representation so that the phase component behaves correctly for intermediate order terms. In systems with one known conservation law, this transformation can be achieved by identifying an appropriate integral invariant. In systems with two known conservation laws, however, this role is filled by the Hamiltonian itself. With this generalized method, we have derived specific equations used in the quasiclassical approximation. These involve new 'nonlinear mixing' terms generated from the higher conservation laws, similar to the 'linear mixing' terms generated from the one conservation law. These terms cause smooth initial data to spread at a faster rate than predicted by linearized chaos, specifically with a speed determined by the highest order law. Additionally, we have found that these terms become significant further in time than the linear mixing terms. We have also numerically verified the accuracy of these approximations. With double conservation laws, solving the full Hamilton-Jacobi equation directly is more feasible than for systems with only one known conservation law, thus making it practical to use higher order approximations to improve accuracy. Our findings show that these approximations provide a more precise prediction of data spreading than the existing methods. This includes the case of the 3D vorticity equations with a constant external force, often used as a benchmark test for conservative systems. In systems with multiple conservation laws and an explicitly known Hamiltonian, such as the Euler equations with an external force, our method can be applied directly to derive the exact quasiclassical approximation. This exact approximation predicts that smooth initial data will spread at a rate determined by the highest order conservation law, specifically the Hamiltonian itself, which we have verified numerically. With systems that are nearly integrable, such as the Euler equations with a random potential, our method can be applied to derive the exact quasiclassical approximation for an infinitely long time. This exact approximation predicts that smooth initial data will spread at a rate determined by the highest order conservation law, which we have numerically verified. This result contradicts the conventional view that smooth initial data will spread at the rate predicted by linearized chaos. With systems that are not nearly integrable, such as the Euler equations with a non-random potential, our method can be applied for a shorter period of time than systems with only one known conservation law, specifically until the nonlinearity becomes significant

Since FD devices can transmit and receive data at the same time, this technology offers improved quality of experience (QoE) through reduced latency and higher data rates. As a result, there is growing interest in developing devices that can operate in FD modes, which has created a need for reliable channel estimation methods. This paper presents a novel deep learning-based approach, termed ultra-wideband deep learning-based (UW-DL) estimator, for calculating the 3GPP FD channel impulse response. By leveraging a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture and exploiting statistical knowledge about the signal, this estimator can accurately determine the uplink and downlink channel impulse responses even in the presence of severe interference. Furthermore, the proposed estimator can support multiple standards by modifying the neural network, as shown in the paper. Additionally, we examine the impact of various parameters on the performance of the UW-DL estimator, providing detailed training guidelines. Moreover, we compare the proposed estimator to a conventional 3GPP FD estimation method, termed element-space (ES) estimator, and show that it outperforms it by achieving a higher accuracy of 54.16 dB and a greater signal-to-interference ratio of 27.15 dB. the success of software development teams.  Researchers have long sought to identify the optimal team structure for various development tasks.  As the industry shifts towards microservices architecture, understanding modern software development team compositions has become increasingly important.  By analyzing data from several popular open-source projects built using microservices architecture, we derived key characteristics of the involved developer teams.  Our analysis revealed notable differences between teams developing individual microservices and those responsible for the overall software architecture.  Notably, we found that while application developers focus primarily on writing new code, system architects tend to dedicate more time to documenting the software structure and reviewing other developers' work.  Our results also indicated that team composition factors such as team size and communication efficiency can significantly impact development efficiency.  By identifying factors such as code reuse and revision difficulties that influence the overall project, we were able to lay the groundwork for future investigations into the dynamics of software development teams.  Our study's findings are presented through visual analytics dashboards that provide an intuitive understanding of the complex structures and interactions within modern software development teams.  By combining quantitative analysis with interactive visualization, we offer a comprehensive overview of the compositions, collaboration patterns, and development challenges experienced by developers working on large-scale, distributed software systems.  Our approach is broadly applicable to the study of software development communities, as documented in our methodological guidelines, which can be used by developers to set up their own metrics frameworks and view their own development team compositions.  Our accompanying discussion section explores potential design improvements for the development of large-scale, distributed software systems, as informed by our analysis of popular open-source projects such as Google's Kubernetes and Netflix's Spinnaker.  By identifying antipatterns in our findings, we are able to provide recommendations for improving the composition and collaboration of development teams, as depicted in our reference architectures.  Ultimately, our study highlights the importance of considering the structural and relational aspects of software development communities, as they play a critical role in shaping the success of project outcomes.  Through our analysis of source code repositories, we identified patterns in developer activity that are associated with known antipatterns and patterns in software architecture, as determined by our analysis of design files.  By linking developer activity to architecture patterns, we provided a compositional view of the development process, by showing how individual developers contribute to the composition of software architectures through a range of actions, as defined in our data analytics framework.  Our results showed that communication and coordination play a critical role in the development of complex software systems, as evidenced by our data

  We demonstrate that in this case, the amplitude of the primordial curvature perturbation can be influenced by the anisotropic effects, however this depends on the characteristics of the post-inflationary universe.

object - black hole binary mergers are examined in a study which goes beyond the current application of the "effective one-body" model to such events. A key discovery found is that when using the "reduced" version of this model, which is suited for fast computations, the alignment of the objects' spins influences their motion in a way that is dependent on how relativistic the event is. This effect on motion is small compared to other factors influencing it and therefore, according to the study, any inaccuracy in modeling this effect using the "reduced" model should be minimal in the near future when observing such events with gravitational waves. Additionally, the study provides a method for calculating the radiation of gravitational waves during the binary's approach, which is based on the "reduced" model. This leads to a better understanding of how the two objects interact and results in a more accurate prediction of the event's parameters observable through gravitational waves. However, the study couldn't determine the binary's final outcome due to its limitations, which are based on the "reduced" model and don't account for the effects of gravitational waves on the binary's evolution. This means that while the study can estimate the event's parameters from a distance, it can't accurately model the approach of two black holes or a black hole and a massive object with significant spins. Any inaccuracy in modeling this effect using the "reduced" model would be minimal in the near future when observing such events with gravitational waves. Furthermore, the study provides a method for randomly generating realistic scenarios of such events which can be used to test the accuracy of computational models of gravitational waves. This will be particularly useful in the near future when observing such events with gravitational waves, which will include superdense matter and potentially solitons, and in testing the accuracy of computational models of gravitational waves through comparisons with actual data. If detected, the event known as GW150604, which was partially detected by the LIGO, could provide valuable information about the nature of dense objects in the form of their density and pressure. However, the study shows that any computational model of this event or similar events must be tested for its accuracy before being used to infer the nature of dense objects, which is because of the significant uncertainty in modeling the effect of gravitational waves on the binary's evolution and the resulting massive object's spin and contraction. Any inaccuracy in modeling this effect would significantly impact the prediction of the event's parameters observable through gravitational waves and the interpretation of similar events which could potentially be detected in the near future.

To better comprehend the Crab pulsar and its surrounding environment, it is crucial to understand the properties of the supernova that gave birth to it. Although the general consensus is that the Crab nebula resulted from a supernova, the type of that explosion has remained uncertain. Our proposed research aims to use very high energy gamma-ray observations of the Crab pulsar to find evidence that can resolve this issue. Due to the narrow beam of the pulsar's gamma-ray emissions, it is possible to perform a detailed background subtraction which can reveal a potential spectral feature at an energy cutoff. To assess this possibility, we conducted a previous analysis with the 2019 data set of the Crab pulsar from the MAGIC telescope, yielding an estimated energy cutoff of approximately 87 TeV, which we used to determine the overall energy output of the pulsar's gamma-ray emissions. In this study, we incorporated new data from the 2018 to 2020 observation periods, which we analyzed in conjunction with the 2019 data from the MAGIC telescope. As a result, we obtained an estimated energy cutoff of 92 TeV, confirming our previous finding and providing a more comprehensive understanding of the pulsar's gamma-ray emissions. Combining this outcome with other properties of the Crab pulsar, we were able to examine the potential of detecting an energy cutoff and its implications for resolving the debate about the type of the Crab supernova. Despite not having sufficient statistics to thoroughly investigate different energy cutoff values, we found that one with an absolute value of around 92 TeV is preferred by the data, which however also allows for a sign change that could be compatible with an origin of the Crab supernova in a supernova explosion within a dense neutron star wind, likely as a result of a low-mass X-ray binary system. By analyzing the conductivity tensors within the nearest-neighbor tight-binding model and comparing the results to a more comprehensive third-neighbor interaction model, we demonstrate that the electronic conductivity is unaffected by the degree of next-neighbor interaction. Conversely, the thermal conductivity, calculated via the kinetic theory of gases, exhibits notable variation with next-neighbor interaction, thereby complicating the expectation that armchair ribbons possess isotropic thermal conductivity. These findings possess critical implications for both the experimental measurement and theoretical analysis of armchair graphene nanoribbons, emphasizing the necessity of considering intercarrier interactions when interpreting experimental data. Moreover, we demonstrate that even minimal impurities can drastically impact the thermal and electrical conductivity, distinguishing this from the behavior of bulk graphene. A key consequence of these findings is the possibility of ballistic transport despite the confinement of the ribbon, especially when the width exceeds the mean free path. As a result, attempts to deduce the dimensionality of the transport based on the conductivity exponent may be compromised, with new guidelines provided. Ultimately, our analysis may also apply to other confined graphene geometries, such as folds and bilayers.

A method of correcting for systematic selection biases was applied, taking into account the relationship between the cross-sectional data and underlying population distribution. This approach involves estimating the average number of galaxies above a given mass threshold within a given volume, and using that as a proxy for completeness. With this technique, the overall luminosity functions and separate ones for "fast" and "slow" galaxies - classified by their star formation rates - were calculated and shown to follow a power-law distribution. The results indicate a distinct difference in the behavior of "fast" and "slow" galaxies at < 10.5 units of solar mass, with a sharp decrease in the number of "fast" galaxies within this mass range. In addition, a comparison with the latest high-resolution dark matter particle simulations revealed a significant discrepancy in the predicted relationships between galaxy properties and the masses of their surrounding halos. Further research is needed to clarify this discrepancy, with a focus on accounting for the systematic characteristics of the observed galaxy population and the mechanisms responsible for their attachment to host halos. In that context, the current study offers a starting point for exploring the evolution of galaxy populations at z < 1.6, with potential applications to interpreting future observations from the James Webb Space Telescope in conjunction with ongoing particle simulations. Lastly, the implications of these findings for the definition of the "galaxy-star" relation and its role in determining major-merger rates are also examined. With this understanding, the average stellar mass assembly history of the typical z ~ 0.5 galaxy is estimated and shown to be in line with the findings of other researchers using different methods. The results of this analysis also suggest that the massive galaxies with black holes at their centers have a mass growth rate roughly 5 times faster than what would be expected from the merger rate of equal-mass pairs, with a significant increase in the mass added to these galaxies through major mergers above the 10.5 unit of solar mass threshold. This research establishes a new method for measuring the thermodynamic efficiency of driven quantum systems, based on their behavior in two specific states of operation - high-drive experiments and low-drive experiments. Using a two-level system as an example, it's shown that even though the system may not reach a steady state due to a large drive, a steady state can still be achieved at lower drive strengths. To ensure these capabilities are also employed for less frequent words, a method is proposed here for learning attention weights based on both local similarities between words and their global relevance.  This approach is an extension of previous research that utilized shared transformers for both local similarity assessment and global context consideration.  By developing a novel multi-task learning approach for the parameters responsible for global context consideration, it is possible to transfer learned context representations to multiple tasks.  This is achieved through shared parameters between the local similarity assessment transformer and a global encoder consisting of two components: one that generates global context and another that evaluates the similarity between words based on given labels.  A similar multi-task learning approach is also described for systems utilizing hierarchical attention mechanisms. concise visual summary of a lengthy video, a challenging task that has been ongoing for several years. This paper introduces a new, unprecedented aspect - creating a written summary of a video and presenting it as a narrated video - with the assistance of pre-trained language models. We acknowledge that producing high-quality written summaries that accurately reflect the contents of a video is a complex task. Nonetheless, with the advancement of deep learning technology, specifically pre-trained models like ALBERT and BERT that excel at understanding natural language, we believe that written summaries can be generated with greater precision. This paper focuses on two aspects: a) a method to create static written summaries of video content; b) an approach to integrate the generated summaries back into the original video as narrations. To achieve this, we employed two techniques: masked language modeling and next sentence prediction. Numerous experiments using the MSVD dataset indicated that our proposed approach can produce high-quality written summaries regardless of the length of the video. Furthermore, the generated summaries can be integrated back into the video as narrations, providing a more engaging viewing experience for users. With the incorporation of pre-trained language models, our proposed approach can handle longer video segments with greater effectiveness, a significant advancement over existing methods. A comparative analysis of our results with those published previously demonstrated our method's superiority, achieving the best overall results. Specifically, our approach outperformed existing models by at least 5% in terms of accuracy, a significant margin. Additionally, we conducted user evaluation studies on both short and extended video segments, the results of which confirmed that the generated summaries were acceptable from a linguistic perspective. Moreover, users were able to comprehend the contents of the video from the provided summaries, a finding supported by our data. A notable aspect emerged from our analysis - users were able to comprehend the contents of the video from the provided summaries at a rate of 53.4%, however they were unable to accurately predict the video's duration from the provided summaries. Moreover, our data revealed that users were able to comprehend the contents of the video from the provided summaries due to the presence of keyframes that helped them, a finding that could be of value to other researchers in the field. A thorough examination of our results in relation to previous research is provided, incorporating both qualitative and quantitative analysis of the summaries generated. A notable aspect emerged from our analysis - the summaries generated were of high quality, a finding that could be of value to other researchers in the field. A comparison of our metrics with those published previously confirmed our approach outperformed existing models

assessing model performance and the impact of specific factors on weather and climate models.  By comparing different approaches to ensemble analysis, researchers can identify the advantages and limitations of various techniques.  This study assesses the methods employed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM) using the Democratic Republic of Congo as a test area.  The evaluation involves analyzing forecasts of atmospheric conditions, precipitation, and temperature, as well as the use of ensemble spread in model assessment.  The findings indicate that the ECMWF's use of the rank histogram and bias measure can evaluate the quality of their forecasts, while the IITM's reliance on the continuous score metric is more effective for this purpose.  The comparison of precipitation forecast forecasts demonstrates that the methods employed by the ECMWF outperform those of the IITM due to an issue with the IITM's model, which overlooks certain precipitation types.  When assessing the impact of model resolution, the researchers found that increasing the resolution to 10.5 km reduces temperature forecast bias but has no significant effect on precipitation forecast bias.  Furthermore, enhancing the model resolution to 10.5 km leads to a notable reduction in dry spell precipitation forecast bias but has no significant advantage in terms of wet spell precipitation forecast bias.  The analysis also highlights the value of using ensemble spread in model assessment, demonstrating that it correlates with forecast bias and provides insights into the effectiveness of various techniques.  Finally, the study emphasizes the importance of validating these methods against observational data in the model assessment process.  The assessment of the ECMWF and IITM models presented in this study can be utilized as a best practice for evaluating the performance of models employed by other African countries with limited ensemble analysis.  The findings of this research can be adapted and implemented in the review process of model performance for the FAO African Monsoon Multidisciplinary Analysis (AMMA) initiative.  The study provides an in-depth analysis of how ensemble analysis can be employed to assess the impact of model resolution on forecast performance, an essential step in the process of enhancing models employed by the ECMWF and the IITM, and can also be utilized as a best practice for evaluating the performance of models employed by other African countries with limited ensemble analysis.  The analysis of the relationship between ensemble spread and forecast bias provides an opportunity for the research to be presented at the upcoming AMMA workshop focused on model assessment, which is scheduled to take place in Niamey

$2$-dimensional scattering system introduced by Hintz and the  2nd and 3rd authors, consisting of two interacting waves where one wave's strength can be made arbitrarily small. We demonstrate that by doing so, the scatterer's shape has significantly less room for variation, ultimately leading to the conclusion that the system must experience a phase transition of a new type. This new type of transition is characterized by a sudden increase in the dispersal of waves at a specific point, and is shown here to occur as the small wave's strength is reduced further and further, provided that the scatterer's shape is roughly a flat disk. This finding is also shown to be a more extensive consequence of a new technical result. Additionally, we provide an analytical explanation for why making the small wave's strength arbitrarily small has such a profound effect on the system, by creating a new type of transition even when the other wave is allowed to vary freely, as long as the system's shape is as smooth as required by Hintz's previous work. Finally, we demonstrate that all of these new results also apply when the system is confined to a limited space. satellite launched in 2022 $-$ will provide precise optical and near-infrared photometry for hundreds of millions of galaxies across different cosmic epochs. The subsequent ground-breaking data will enable accurate measurements of several key cosmological parameters. This study represents the fifth in a series where we examine various aspects of Euclid observations. Here, we focus on the distribution of redshifts for $10^{8}$ simulated galaxy populations, emphasizing how the choice of prior probabilities influences the determination of the distribution's parameters. We initially consider a one-dimensional redshift distribution, later introducing a cutoff at higher values. The chosen parameters are then scaled according to the Euclid mission's expected characteristics. We simulated $10^{8}$ independent galaxy populations, calculating their average and dispersion for key distribution parameters across different prior options. We observed that, under optimal conditions with minimal photometric noise and no saturation, the estimated parameters remain relatively stable for all prior choices. However, this stability is compromised when considering two more realistic scenarios: one with increased saturation levels and another with more significant photometric variability. While the associated parameter deviations remain minimal in the first scenario, they become more significant in the second, indicating a potential limitation for Euclid. Additionally, we investigated the distribution of extended objects' lengths as seen by the satellite, establishing a statistical model that can be used for future research. The chosen configuration with scaled parameters is applicable to approximately 350 million Euclid observations, covering a broad range of prior probabilities. The relationships we simulated can be adapted for alternative prior choices. To mitigate this, we explore an alternative strategy that achieves similar privacy protection through a different mechanism, which is shown to result in more favorable variance behavior. By comparing these results, we highlight the design choices involved in balancing performance and privacy in XAV control. Our analysis involves a detailed examination of the elastic and inelastic properties of magnetic excitations, starting with a general representation of their dispersion.   The anisotropy of magnetic excitation dynamics in layered materials arises from their unique crystallographic and magnetic structures, which dictate the behavior of adjacent atomic planes. This interplane interaction is inherently anisotropic due to varying in-plane magnetic order and crystallographic misalignment at opposing atomic interfaces. As a result, this interaction fuels anisotropic magnetic excitation dynamics across multiple length scales, as seen in the elastic and inelastic properties of these materials. 

  In this study, we investigate the anisotropic dynamics of magnetic excitations in transition metal dichalcogenides and strontium manganate. These materials exhibit unique excitation behavior that is driven by very close magnetic interaction energies and diverse in-plane magnetic orders, presenting a complex scenario for experimental analysis. 

  To begin with, we explore a general representation of magnetic excitation dispersion, which can be broken down into three distinct components: a flat band representing low-energy, quasi-two-dimensional magnetic excitations; a three-dimensional magnetic excitation branch characterized by a parabolic energy profile; and a high-energy branch exhibiting different anisotropy patterns. 

  The anisotropy of magnetic excitation dynamics is closely linked to the orientation-dependent elastic properties, as expressed by the magnetic excitation elasticity equation that takes into account the change in excitation energy with angle.

This model has two active modes of behavior which lead to distinct wave propagation scenarios, either purely hyperbolic or elliptic, depending on the specific input parameters used. A numerical analysis is performed to examine the propagation of waves in both of these modes, resulting in a set of unique solutions for both cases. A key observation from our study indicates that non-harmonic wave solutions can occur at frequencies below a certain cutoff value, while harmonic wave solutions are found at frequencies above this threshold. A key feature of the Gieskes model is its ability to mimic the behavior of complex materials whose constitutive equations cannot be accurately represented without considering the spatial and temporal context, which is referred to as 'contextuality'. This property of the Gieskes model allows it to differentiate from other similar models, such as the Gieskes-Li Sun model, which lacks contextuality. As a result, the Gieskes model is able to produce more realistic simulations for certain types of experiments. Additionally, our study highlights that even in situations where the Gieskes model produces similar results to the Gieskes-Li Sun model, the former is still the more appropriate choice due to its better alignment with the actual properties of the materials being studied, even though this difference may not be noticeable at the scale of current experiments. Lastly, our study also addresses an open question regarding the possibility of solutions losing stability as the material's strength decreases below a certain threshold, and provides a new definition for this concept, as well as a graphical representation of this phenomenon in the available data sets. To comprehend how VWB spreads through honeybee colonies, research typically relies on simulations or experimental colony observations.  However, these methods usually overlook the mites' intricate life cycle, which dictates their movement between bees.  To address this gap, this study presents a mathematical model accounting for the complex relationships between VWB-infected bees, Varroa mites, and wax removal behavior by the bees in response to high mite densities.  This model incorporates the precise lifespan and life stage transformations of the mites and incorporates the effects of DWV on bee behavior. These hotspots are characterized by the presence of infected bees displaying the "emergency room behavior" associated with high mite densities, thereby highlighting their potential as a key factor in promoting VWB transmission through the colony.  This understanding can be used to improve the effectiveness of mite control measures and to develop predictive models of VWB transmission dynamics and colony responses.  By exploring how these results apply to two previous models, we also provide corresponding models modified to incorporate the "emergency room behavior" and analyze the impact of these modifications on the models' solutions.  This research is complemented by a publicly accessible database containing the results of a wide-ranging experiment involving 64 different bee colonies, covering various factors such as VWB infection levels, mite populations, bee behavior associated with high mite densities, and colony responses to interventions. With the rise of large-scale medical datasets and sophisticated neural network models, artificial intelligence-powered bots can now mimic physician-patient conversations with remarkable realism. However, ensuring these online discussions are both legally compliant and clinically effective is a pressing concern. In this research, we explore current regulatory frameworks and clinical guidelines for online healthcare conversations, identifying key requirements that both human healthcare professionals and artificial intelligence-powered bots must meet. Furthermore, we highlight existing evaluation metrics for assessing the effectiveness of online healthcare conversations and suggest potential areas for future improvement. With the aim of stimulating innovative research in this domain, we release a new dataset called MedChatEval, consisting of 500 dialogue segments annotated with relevance, accuracy, and overall quality. This dataset encompasses a wide range of topics and situations, encompassing critical evaluations that pose a significant challenge for any machine learning-based scoring system to pass. We also present a comprehensive evaluation of 11 diverse models, utilizing both a model-specific scoring system and an externally available one for comparison. Using this approach, we examine how the probability of black hole formation changes during different phases of inflation and assess its relationship with the scalar perturbation power spectrum. Consignment UAVs often carry valuable payloads on their return journey, making them attractive targets for malicious actors. Additionally, UAVs can be programmed to follow complex mission protocols, which may be compromised by cyber attacks. 

  This study introduces a novel approach to safeguard UAV delivery missions against cyber threats by utilizing formal verification and dynamic information flow. Our approach involves embedding security requirements into mission protocols, which dynamically filter sensitive information to prevent cyber attacks and minimize the system's overall complexity while maintaining protocol correctness.

  We demonstrate the practicality of this approach through a real-world example utilizing the ACASXU (Airborne Conflict Resolution using Interval Methods) protocol and the CVX3 tool from the CVX3 toolset, which successfully verifies the security of a complex UAV delivery mission. 

  We also compare our approach to another method by conducting a case study on the Birdstrike Avoidance System, which shows that our approach has a tolerable impact on computational resources and can handle more complex systems.

This study proposes an accelerated particle beam consisting of two parts: the inner circle, where collisions occur, maintained by nonlinear motion, and an outer layer, responsible for overall beam stability, maintained by circular motion. This prototype, incorporating a nonlinear beam in the klystron, would allow scientists to study the interplay between beam and photon interactions when a high-energy, curved electron beam is forced to make a sudden change in motion by a pulse of intense X-rays. This study investigates the possibility of using approximate near neighbors of a point in a graph under the general Hamilton-Wielandt distance.  Specifically, we define a $c$-$\epsilon$ approximate near neighbor as a point with a distance of at most $c\epsilon$ from the original point, where $c$ represents the ratio of the maximum possible value in the graph.  Our main contribution involves demonstrating the existence of an efficient algorithm for identifying $c$-$\epsilon$ approximate near neighbors in both unweighted and weighted graphs.  This algorithm's efficiency is guaranteed regardless of the data set's size or the value of $\epsilon$, but it varies with the value of $c$.  In certain cases, where $\epsilon$ tends towards zero at a rate of $1/\sqrt{n}$ or better, our results meet the requirements set by the Vanishing Successors Conjecture first proposed in (Parnas and Zick, FOCS 2015).  Furthermore, our research involves developing a new data structure, referred to as a HW-Set, that incorporates two existing data structures, HH Sketch and HW Distance Sketch, where HW-Set allows for the efficient identification of approximate near neighbors.  Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of implementing the HW-Set data structure across various contexts.  Our study lays the groundwork for further research into algorithms that rely on approximate near neighbors and provides a starting point for exploring the Vanishing Successors Conjecture in (Parnas and Zick, FOCS 2015).  In particular, we propose answering the question of whether the HW-Set data structure can be constructed in an efficient manner, where efficiency is defined by an exponential relationship with the inverse of $\epsilon$.
